Cairo-Egypt.name: Cairo
Cairo-Egypt.evidence_basis: Combined Al-Qahira and Fustat conurbation assessed from built-up intramural and suburban area under al-Nasir Muhammad (~800-950 ha at 400-450/ha), Black Death mortality of ~40%, and late Mamluk recovery (Raymond 2000; Dols 1977; Borsch 2005; al-Maqrizi).

Fez-Morocco.name: Fez
Fez-Morocco.evidence_basis: Unified by the Almoravids into ~280 ha Fes el-Bali and expanded in 1276 with royal Fes Jdid as Marinid imperial capital; assessed from urban area, guild/mosque inventories, Black Death impact, and Leo Africanus's detailed quarter survey (Le Tourneau 1961; Bennison 2016).

Marrakech-Morocco.name: Marrakech
Marrakech-Morocco.evidence_basis: Founded c. 1070 by the Almoravids and expanded with a vast khettara-irrigated rampart circuit and 36 ha Almohad royal Kasbah; peaked under the Almohads before contracting steeply after the 1269 Marinid shift of the capital to Fez (Deverdun 1959; Bennison 2016; Leo Africanus).

Tunis-Tunisia.name: Tunis
Tunis-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Rose from a Zirid port to the Almohad and Hafsid imperial capital enclosing ~270 ha (medina plus Bab Souika and Bab al-Jazira suburbs), swollen by Andalusian exiles and European fondouks; Leo Africanus estimated ~10,000 inner hearths plus vast suburbs (Brunschvig 1940; Daoulatli 1976).

Kairouan-Tunisia.name: Kairouan
Kairouan-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Zirid capital encompassing the medina and the 111 ha Fatimid-Zirid palace-city of Sabra al-Mansuriya until the catastrophic 1057 Banu Hilal sack reduced it to a modest provincial religious and carpet-weaving centre under the Hafsids (Cressier & Rammah 2006; Brunschvig 1940; Fenwick 2020).

Tlemcen-Algeria.name: Tlemcen
Tlemcen-Algeria.evidence_basis: Zayyanid (Abd al-Wadid) imperial capital unifying Agadir and Almoravid Tagrart into a dense trans-Saharan and Mediterranean emporium; Leo Africanus records 16,000 hearths at its zenith declining to ~12,000 by 1515 (Marçais 1954; Leo Africanus).

Alexandria-Egypt.name: Alexandria
Alexandria-Egypt.evidence_basis: Assessed from medieval walled perimeter contraction, Karimi Mediterranean spice-port revenues, severe 1348 plague mortality, and the devastating 1365 Cypriot Crusade sack followed by partial Qaitbay-era recovery (Dols 1977; Udovitch 1978; Borsch 2005).

Bejaia-Algeria.name: Bejaia
Bejaia-Algeria.evidence_basis: Founded in 1067 as Hammadid al-Nasiriyya and major Hafsid maritime emporium for Pisan, Genoese, and Catalan trade (~8,000 hearths per Leo Africanus in 1500) before the 1510 Spanish conquest caused mass flight (Valérian 2006; Golvin 1957).

Ceuta-Morocco.name: Ceuta
Ceuta-Morocco.evidence_basis: Premier Strait of Gibraltar commercial and naval entrepôt boasting paper mills, coral trade, and Italian merchant fondouks under the Almoravids, Almohads, Azafids, and Marinids until the 1415 Portuguese conquest expelled its Muslim urban populace (al-Idrisi; Latham 1973).

Qus-Egypt.name: Qus
Qus-Egypt.evidence_basis: Upper Egypt administrative capital and Nile terminus for the Aydhab Red Sea spice and Hajj route; rose sharply after 1050 and declined steadily after the 1348 plague, Bedouin unrest, and the 1426 destruction of Aydhab (Garcin 1976).

Al-Mahdiyya-Tunisia.name: Al-Mahdiyya
Al-Mahdiyya-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Fortified Fatimid peninsular capital plus walled mercantile suburb of Zwaila that peaked as the Zirid refuge seat after 1057 before declining following the 1148 Norman occupation, 1160 Almohad siege, and 1390 Franco-Genoese assault (Lézine 1965; Brunschvig 1940).

Sijilmasa-Morocco.name: Sijilmasa
Sijilmasa-Morocco.evidence_basis: Great northern terminus of the trans-Saharan gold trade anchored by a 100 km² canal-irrigated Tafilalt palmery and 5 km urban axis; declined after Ma'qil Arab disruption and fragmented after the 1393 destruction into dispersed oasis qsur (Lightfoot & Miller 1996; Messier & Miller 2015).

Meknes-Morocco.name: Meknes
Meknes-Morocco.evidence_basis: Wealthy Saiss agricultural and olive-oil city expanded with Almohad walls and Marinid madrasas; Leo Africanus explicitly records 6,000 families (~30,000 residents) c. 1515 (al-Idrisi; Leo Africanus).

Constantine-Algeria.name: Constantine
Constantine-Algeria.evidence_basis: Formidable Rhumel-gorge citadel and principal eastern Algerian grain, wool, and leather hub under Hammadid, Almohad, and Hafsid governors; credited with ~8,000 hearths by Leo Africanus (~40,000 inhabitants) (Brunschvig 1940; Leo Africanus).

Qal'at Bani Hammad-Algeria.name: Qal'at Bani Hammad
Qal'at Bani Hammad-Algeria.evidence_basis: 150 ha Hammadid mountain capital enclosed by a 7 km rampart founded in 1007; declined rapidly after the Hammadid court relocated to Bejaia c. 1090 under Hilalian pressure and was destroyed by the Almohads in 1152 (De Beylié 1909; Golvin 1957; Fenwick 2020).

Damietta-Egypt.name: Damietta
Damietta-Egypt.evidence_basis: Eastern Nile Delta linen-exporting port and fortress; suffered catastrophic Fifth (1219) and Seventh (1249) Crusade sieges and 1250 Mamluk inland relocation before rebounding in late Mamluk Mediterranean trade (al-Maqrizi; Cooper 2014; Leo Africanus).

Tinnis-Egypt.name: Tinnis
Tinnis-Egypt.evidence_basis: Walled Lake Manzala island tiraz textile metropolis covering ~93 ha with densely packed looms and cisterns; declined under Sicilian/Crusader raids, partially evacuated in 1192, and finally demolished by Sultan al-Kamil in 1227 (Gascoigne 2007; Cooper 2014).

Tripoli-Libya.name: Tripoli
Tripoli-Libya.evidence_basis: Walled Tripolitanian maritime capital (~48 ha medina) prospering on Genoese/Venetian and Fezzan caravan trade under Banu Khazrun, Hafsids, and Banu Thabit; severely disrupted by the 1146 Norman and 1510 Spanish conquests (al-Idrisi; Brunschvig 1940; Leo Africanus).

Sale-Morocco.name: Sale
Sale-Morocco.evidence_basis: Major Bou Regreg Atlantic port, wool-textile exporter, and Marinid naval arsenal (dar al-sina'a) visited by Genoese and Castilian merchants; suffered a brief 1260 Castilian raid before peaking in the 14th century (Ibn al-Khatib; Brown 1976; Leo Africanus).

Oran-Algeria.name: Oran
Oran-Algeria.evidence_basis: Principal Zayyanid maritime port enriched by Catalan, Venetian, and Genoan commerce and Andalusian refugees (~6,000 hearths recorded by Leo Africanus before the destructive 1509 Spanish conquest).

Al-Mahalla al-Kubra-Egypt.name: Al-Mahalla al-Kubra
Al-Mahalla al-Kubra-Egypt.evidence_basis: Principal inland capital of Gharbiyya province and major central Delta textile and agricultural tax hub insulated from coastal raids; assessed from Mamluk iqta and diwan records (al-Maqrizi; Ibn Duqmaq; Borsch 2005).

Algiers-Algeria.name: Algiers
Algiers-Algeria.evidence_basis: Medium-sized Zirid and Zayyanid port (~4,000 hearths recorded by Leo Africanus c. 1500, corroborated by Cresti) that grew rapidly after 1492 with Andalusian exiles and the 1516-1517 arrival of the Barbarossa corsairs (Raymond 2002; Leo Africanus).

Tangier-Morocco.name: Tangier
Tangier-Morocco.evidence_basis: Strait of Gibraltar transit port and birthplace of Ibn Battuta thriving under Almoravid, Almohad, and Marinid maritime networks until the 1471 Portuguese occupation reduced it to a heavily garrisoned coastal enclave (al-Idrisi; Leo Africanus).

Sousse-Tunisia.name: Sousse
Sousse-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Aghlabid-Zirid naval base and olive-oil port enclosed by a 32 ha defensive enceinte (Lézine 1956; Fenwick 2020); suffered late Hafsid maritime raids and depopulation noted by Leo Africanus around 1515.

Asyut-Egypt.name: Asyut
Asyut-Egypt.evidence_basis: Major Upper Egyptian woollen-textile centre and Darb al-Arba'in caravan terminus that rose in administrative importance under Sultan Barquq as seat of an Upper Egypt niyaba during Qus's decline (Garcin 1976; al-Maqrizi; Leo Africanus).

Rabat-Morocco.name: Rabat
Rabat-Morocco.evidence_basis: Founded in 1150 by Almohad Caliph Abd al-Mu'min and walled on a grand imperial scale (~420 ha planned circuit) by Yaqub al-Mansur for Andalusian expeditions; contracted sharply after Almohad decline, with Leo Africanus noting most of the walled area stood vacant.

Taza-Morocco.name: Taza
Taza-Morocco.evidence_basis: Strategic highland fortress controlling the Taza Gap between Fez and Tlemcen, walled by the Almohads and endowed with Marinid madrasas; Leo Africanus notes a thriving market city including ~500 Jewish houses alone.

Aghmat-Morocco.name: Aghmat
Aghmat-Morocco.evidence_basis: Pre-Almoravid twin capital of the Haouz plain with extensive excavated baths, palaces, and irrigated gardens (Cressier & González Villaescusa 2019; al-Bakri); gradually eclipsed after Marrakech's 1070 founding until reduced to a small market town by 1500 (Leo Africanus).

Sfax-Tunisia.name: Sfax
Sfax-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Compact walled medina (~24 ha plus dense extramural garden belts) thriving on Sahel olive oil, wool-fulling, and fisheries; experienced brief Norman rule (1148-1156) and steady Hafsid commercial vitality (al-Idrisi; Brunschvig 1940; Leo Africanus).

Faiyum-Egypt.name: Faiyum
Faiyum-Egypt.evidence_basis: Provincial capital of the irrigated Fayyum oasis basin documented in al-Nabulusi's detailed 1245 fiscal and canal survey (Tarikh al-Fayyum) and post-Black Death irrigation decay assessments (Rapoport & Shahar 2012; Borsch 2005).

Safi-Morocco.name: Safi
Safi-Morocco.evidence_basis: Principal Atlantic harbour of Marrakech and Abda grain/wax export port (~4,000 houses reported by Leo Africanus before the 1508 Portuguese occupation triggered civilian emigration).

Bilbays-Egypt.name: Bilbays
Bilbays-Egypt.evidence_basis: Sharqiyya provincial seat and fortified eastern Delta staging post on the Syria highway; sacked by Crusaders in 1168 and heavily depopulated in the 1348 Black Death as chronicled by al-Maqrizi (Dols 1977; Borsch 2005).

Azemmour-Morocco.name: Azemmour
Azemmour-Morocco.evidence_basis: Wealthy Oum Er-Rbia estuary port renowned for Doukkala grain exports and lucrative shad fisheries trading with Portugal; Leo Africanus depicts a densely populated town prior to the 1513 Portuguese conquest.

Gabes-Tunisia.name: Gabes
Gabes-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Walled coastal oasis city famed for irrigated palm groves, silk-rearing, and henna exports under the Banu Jami and Hafsid governors (al-Bakri; al-Idrisi; Brunschvig 1940).

Rosetta-Egypt.name: Rosetta
Rosetta-Egypt.evidence_basis: Western Nile-mouth port that grew steadily during the 15th century as Alexandria's connecting canal silted and Sultan Qaitbay fortified the harbour in 1479; visited and described as bustling by Leo Africanus in 1517 (Cooper 2014; Raymond 2000).

Barqa-Libya.name: Barqa
Barqa-Libya.evidence_basis: Principal medieval Cyrenaican administrative and agricultural town in the 10th-11th centuries (al-Bakri; Abdussaid excavations) that contracted steeply after the post-1051 Banu Sulaym pastoralization documented by al-Idrisi and Leo Africanus.

Akhmim-Egypt.name: Akhmim
Akhmim-Egypt.evidence_basis: Historic Upper Egyptian textile-weaving and Coptic-Muslim provincial town described by Ibn Jubayr (1183), Ibn Battuta, and Leo Africanus; suffered post-plague and Bedouin-induced contraction in the late Mamluk era (Garcin 1976).

Annaba-Algeria.name: Annaba
Annaba-Algeria.evidence_basis: Rebuilt 11th-century walled harbour town (Buna al-Haditha) near ancient Hippo serving Hafsid grain, wool, and coral exports to Italy and Marseille (al-Idrisi; Brunschvig 1940; Leo Africanus).

Mansoura-Egypt.name: Mansoura
Mansoura-Egypt.evidence_basis: Founded in 1219 by Ayyubid Sultan al-Kamil as a fortified camp during the Fifth Crusade and site of the 1250 battle against Louis IX; developed into the principal Daqahliyya commercial centre on the Damietta branch (al-Maqrizi; Ibn Duqmaq).

Damanhur-Egypt.name: Damanhur
Damanhur-Egypt.evidence_basis: Capital of Buhayra province in the western Delta and regional cotton, flax, and grain collection market linking Cairo and Alexandria; tracked via Mamluk cadastral rok surveys and Bedouin raid chronicles (al-Maqrizi; Borsch 2005).

Biskra-Algeria.name: Biskra
Biskra-Algeria.evidence_basis: Capital of the Zab oasis province south of the Aures under the Banu Muzni and Hafsids, famous for extensive date palmeries and caravan commerce (al-Bakri; Ibn Khaldun; Leo Africanus).

Taroudant-Morocco.name: Taroudant
Taroudant-Morocco.evidence_basis: Capital of the fertile Sous valley famous for irrigated cane-sugar production, copper working, and caravan exchange; gained renewed prominence in the 1510s as an early Saadian powerbase (al-Idrisi; Rosenberger 1970; Leo Africanus).

Beja-Tunisia.name: Beja
Beja-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Principal wheat granary and fortified Medjerda market town of northern Ifriqiya, supplying Tunis and Genoese grain buyers throughout the Zirid and Hafsid eras (al-Idrisi; Brunschvig 1940; Leo Africanus).

Ksar el-Kebir-Morocco.name: Ksar el-Kebir
Ksar el-Kebir-Morocco.evidence_basis: Fortified Loukkos-plain town rebuilt by Almohad Yaqub al-Mansur as a major military staging base and market for northern Gharb cereals, flax, and textiles (al-Idrisi; Leo Africanus).

Minya-Egypt.name: Minya
Minya-Egypt.evidence_basis: Prosperous Middle Egypt Nile port and sugar-milling/textile town (Munyat Ibn Khasib) praised by Ibn Battuta in 1326 as surpassing all towns of Upper Egypt in civic amenities (Garcin 1976; Ibn Battuta).

Bizerte-Tunisia.name: Bizerte
Bizerte-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Northern Ifriqiyan fortified lagoon port and tuna-fishery emporium described by al-Idrisi and Brunschvig (1940), reinforced in the late 15th century by Andalusian settlers.

Aswan-Egypt.name: Aswan
Aswan-Egypt.evidence_basis: Southern Nile frontier port and Banu al-Kanz seat mediating Nubian trade; contracted sharply after the 1348 plague, repeated Awlad Kanz conflicts, and the 1412 Hawara sack before modest stabilisation by Leo Africanus's visit (Garcin 1976; Leo Africanus).

Tozeur-Tunisia.name: Tozeur
Tozeur-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Chief oasis city of the Bilad al-Jarid date-palm confederation fed by Ibn Chabbat's 13th-century hydraulic division system; praised by al-Bakri, Ibn Battuta, and Leo Africanus for dense brick quarters and caravan trade.

Fuwwa-Egypt.name: Fuwwa
Fuwwa-Egypt.evidence_basis: Rosetta-branch riverine entrepôt and textile-dyeing town that flourished from the 14th to early 16th century as the main transfer port on the Alexandria-Cairo canal and river route (Ibn Duqmaq; Leo Africanus; Cooper 2014).

Surt-Libya.name: Surt
Surt-Libya.evidence_basis: Excavated Fatimid-Zirid walled coastal town (~18-20 ha intramural core with congregational mosque, glass kilns, and forts) that flourished up to 1051 before Hilalian/Sulaym devastation reduced it to a dwindling ruin abandoned by the 14th century (Fehérvari et al. 2002; Mouton & Racinet 2011).

Miliana-Algeria.name: Miliana
Miliana-Algeria.evidence_basis: Fortified Zirid and Zayyanid hill town overlooking the fertile Chelif valley with watermills, weaving workshops, and regional orchards described by al-Idrisi and Leo Africanus.

Oujda-Morocco.name: Oujda
Oujda-Morocco.evidence_basis: Founded in 994 by Ziri ibn Atiyya on the Angad plain; served as a heavily contested frontier town and caravan market between Marinid Fez and Zayyanid Tlemcen (al-Bakri; Ibn Khaldun; Leo Africanus).

Aydhab-Egypt.name: Aydhab
Aydhab-Egypt.evidence_basis: Premier Red Sea spice and Hajj embarkation port during Fatimid, Ayyubid, and early Mamluk periods (Ibn Jubayr; Peacock & Peacock 2008); declined as Red Sea shipping shifted north and was permanently destroyed by Sultan Barsbay in 1426.

Gafsa-Tunisia.name: Gafsa
Gafsa-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Walled spring-irrigated oasis and pistachio/woollen-cloth centre ruled autonomously by the Banu al-Rand before Almohad and Hafsid integration (al-Idrisi; Brunschvig 1940; Leo Africanus).

Tenes-Algeria.name: Tenes
Tenes-Algeria.evidence_basis: Andalusian-founded walled coastal port and seat of an autonomous late-medieval Zayyanid branch exporting Chelif wheat, honey, and wax (al-Bakri; al-Idrisi; Leo Africanus).

Honaine-Algeria.name: Honaine
Honaine-Algeria.evidence_basis: Excavated Almohad and Zayyanid walled port serving as Tlemcen's closest maritime outlet to Almeria and Majorca, featuring fortified harbour basins and merchant fondouks (Khelifa 2008; Leo Africanus).

Ajdabiya-Libya.name: Ajdabiya
Ajdabiya-Libya.evidence_basis: Excavated Fatimid caravan crossroads and walled town featuring a palatial fortress and octagonal-minaret mosque (Blake et al. 1971; al-Bakri); diminished sharply after mid-11th-century Banu Sulaym incursions into a small oasis market (al-Idrisi; Leo Africanus).

Setif-Algeria.name: Setif
Setif-Algeria.evidence_basis: High Plateaux cereal market with excavated 10th-11th-century courtyard-house neighbourhoods and medieval ramparts (Mohamedi et al. 1991; Fenwick 2020) that contracted moderately following 11th-12th-century nomadic disruptions.

Tetouan-Morocco.name: Tetouan
Tetouan-Morocco.evidence_basis: Modest Marinid fortified base destroyed by Castilian forces in 1399; rebuilt in 1484 by Granadan commander Abu al-Hasan al-Mandri and rapidly populated by Andalusian Muslim and Sephardic exiles after 1492 (Leo Africanus).

Esna-Egypt.name: Esna
Esna-Egypt.evidence_basis: Major southern Sa'id market town, caravan waypoint, and centre of Fatimid-Mamluk religious scholarship south of Qus documented by Ibn Jubayr and Garcin's Upper Egypt demographic study (Garcin 1976).

Nedroma-Algeria.name: Nedroma
Nedroma-Algeria.evidence_basis: Walled Trara mountain town and cotton-weaving centre with an 11th-century Almoravid Great Mosque supporting Tlemcen's hinterland and Honaine's port traffic (al-Idrisi; Marçais 1954; Leo Africanus).

Zagora-Morocco.name: Zagora
Zagora-Morocco.evidence_basis: Principal medieval urban centre of the Middle Draa Valley featuring two densely settled walled compounds of 17 ha (Almoravid/Almohad governor garrison) plus surrounding irrigated oasis settlements booming in the 11th-13th centuries and reviving as Sijilmasa declined (Allain & Meunié 1956; Fenwick et al. 2022).

Misrata-Libya.name: Misrata
Misrata-Libya.evidence_basis: Coastal Tripolitanian oasis and port that rose during the 13th-15th centuries as a key terminus linking Venetian/Genoese shipping with the Waddan-Fezzan caravan route (al-Idrisi; Brunschvig 1940; Leo Africanus).

Msila-Algeria.name: Msila
Msila-Algeria.evidence_basis: Fatimid-founded Hodna plain garrison and irrigated grain town (al-Muhammadiyya) flourishing alongside Qal'at Bani Hammad in the 11th century before declining under Hilalian pastoral pressure (al-Bakri; Golvin 1957).

Qalyub-Egypt.name: Qalyub
Qalyub-Egypt.evidence_basis: Administrative seat of Qalyubiyya province and rich agricultural provisioning centre just north of Cairo's canal network; tracked through Mamluk cadastral records (Ibn al-Ji'an; al-Maqrizi).

Medea-Algeria.name: Medea
Medea-Algeria.evidence_basis: Titteri highland fortress-town established by Buluggin ibn Ziri in the late 10th century and maintained as an agricultural and market centre linking the Mitidja plain to the High Plateaux (al-Idrisi; Leo Africanus).

Monastir-Tunisia.name: Monastir
Monastir-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Fortified coastal ribat complex, religious retreat, and Sahel olive port with standing medieval enceinte and mosques analyzed by Lézine (1966) and Brunschvig (1940).

Mostaganem-Algeria.name: Mostaganem
Mostaganem-Algeria.evidence_basis: Walled coastal town near the Chelif mouth fortified under the Almoravids and Marinids (1341 Great Mosque), recorded by Leo Africanus at ~1,500 hearths with active weaving and regional maritime trade.

Beni Suef-Egypt.name: Beni Suef
Beni Suef-Egypt.evidence_basis: Middle Egyptian Nile port and linen-manufacturing town serving the Bahnasa and eastern Fayyum corridors; assessed from Mamluk fiscal registers (Ibn al-Ji'an; al-Maqrizi).

Asilah-Morocco.name: Asilah
Asilah-Morocco.evidence_basis: Walled northern Atlantic port and agricultural market town described by al-Bakri and al-Idrisi; fell sharply after the 1471 Portuguese conquest and enslavement/expulsion of residents (Leo Africanus).

El Kef-Tunisia.name: El Kef
El Kef-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Strategic High Tell fortress controlling the inland corridor between Tunis and Constantine, documented as a fortified provincial seat in Zirid and Hafsid chronicles (al-Idrisi; Brunschvig 1940).

Touggourt-Algeria.name: Touggourt
Touggourt-Algeria.evidence_basis: Capital of the Oued Righ artesian-oasis corridor that expanded during the 14th-15th centuries into the seat of the Banu Jallab Saharan sultanate; described by Ibn Khaldun and Leo Africanus as a fortified palmery town.

Cherchell-Algeria.name: Cherchell
Cherchell-Algeria.evidence_basis: Modest medieval coastal settlement excavated by Potter (1995) that underwent rapid urban revival after 1492 when hundreds of Granadan Morisco families settled to develop silk cultivation and pottery (Leo Africanus).

Girga-Egypt.name: Girga
Girga-Egypt.evidence_basis: Modest medieval Upper Egyptian river town that grew rapidly under late Mamluk Hawwara Arab leadership in the 15th century, positioning it to supersede Qus as Upper Egypt's capital after 1517 (Garcin 1976).

Nefta-Tunisia.name: Nefta
Nefta-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Westernmost oasis city of the Tunisian Jarid famed for abundant artesian springs, date exports, and scholarly zawiya networks (al-Idrisi; Leo Africanus).

Suez-Egypt.name: Suez
Suez-Egypt.evidence_basis: Early Islamic Qulzum declined after the Trajanic-Amr canal silted and trade shifted to Aydhab, then revived sharply as al-Suways under late Mamluk Sultans Qaitbay and Qansuh al-Ghawri as a Red Sea naval shipyard against Portugal (al-Maqrizi; Cooper 2014).

Mazouna-Algeria.name: Mazouna
Mazouna-Algeria.evidence_basis: Dahra mountain commercial and legal-scholarship hub (famed for the 15th-century Al-Durar al-Maknuna fatwa compilation) sustaining woollen weaving and agricultural markets (al-Idrisi; Leo Africanus).

Dellys-Algeria.name: Dellys
Dellys-Algeria.evidence_basis: Walled coastal town between Algiers and Bejaia exporting figs, wool, and dyed fabrics; augmented in the late 15th century by Andalusian migrants as noted by Leo Africanus.

Gharyan-Libya.name: Gharyan
Gharyan-Libya.evidence_basis: Highland Jebel Nafusa agricultural and saffron-producing stronghold guarding the caravan ascent south of Tripoli, noted for dense troglodyte and fortified village clusters (al-Idrisi; Leo Africanus; Barker 1996).

Larache-Morocco.name: Larache
Larache-Morocco.evidence_basis: Loukkos estuary harbour fortified under the Marinids and Wattasids to counter Portuguese expansion along the Atlantic coast, exporting charcoal, cotton, and timber (Leo Africanus).

Jijel-Algeria.name: Jijel
Jijel-Algeria.evidence_basis: Lesser Kabylia fortified port exporting timber, wax, and hides; raided by Norman Sicily in 1143 and later contested by Genoa before becoming Aruj Barbarossa's base in 1514 (al-Idrisi; Valérian 2006; Leo Africanus).

Zliten-Libya.name: Zliten
Zliten-Libya.evidence_basis: Fertile eastern Tripolitanian coastal palmery and olive district near the former Leptis Magna hinterland (Munzi et al. 2014) that expanded in the late 15th century around Sufi zawiya foundations and regional grain trade.

Nabeul-Tunisia.name: Nabeul
Nabeul-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Cap Bon coastal ceramic-producing and horticultural market town continuing urban craft activity through the Zirid and Hafsid periods (al-Idrisi; Fenwick 2020).

Chefchaouen-Morocco.name: Chefchaouen
Chefchaouen-Morocco.evidence_basis: Founded in 1471 by Moulay Ali ibn Rashid as a Rif mountain fortress against Portuguese incursions and rapidly expanded after 1492 by Granadan Morisco and Jewish refugees (Carbonero et al. 1997; Leo Africanus).

Port Tawfîq-Egypt.name: Port Tawfîq
other_names: قسم أول ويتبعها بور توفيق والزيتيات والمنطقة السكنية التابعة لمعمل تكرير البترول الأميري الواقعة بالجزء الشرقي لشريط السكة الحديد

Anfa-Morocco.name: Anfa
Anfa-Morocco.evidence_basis: Wealthy Chaouia grain-exporting harbour and autonomous corsair port documented by al-Idrisi and Marinid chronicles until the Portuguese completely destroyed and depopulated it in 1468 (Leo Africanus records it lying deserted).

Nul Lamta-Morocco.name: Nul Lamta
Nul Lamta-Morocco.evidence_basis: Southwestern Saharan caravan entrepôt on the Wad Nun (archaeologically identified at Asrir near Guelmim) renowned for Almoravid gold minting and Lamta leather shields (al-Bakri; al-Idrisi; De Juan Ares et al. 2011; Fenwick et al. 2022).

Hammamet-Tunisia.name: Hammamet
Hammamet-Tunisia.evidence_basis: Fortified Hafsid coastal port whose compact medina ramparts and kasbah were expanded in the 13th-15th centuries for regional fishing, charcoal, and linen trade (Brunschvig 1940; Leo Africanus).

Waddan-Libya.name: Waddan
Waddan-Libya.evidence_basis: Twin fortified Jufra oasis town with foggara irrigation serving as the northern gateway between Fezzan and the Gulf of Sirte coast (al-Bakri; al-Idrisi; Mattingly et al. 2020; Leo Africanus).

Benghazi-Libya.name: Benghazi
Benghazi-Libya.evidence_basis: Small medieval successor settlement to Berenice (Berniq) during the 11th-14th centuries that was refounded and expanded in the mid-15th century as Marsa Ibn Ghazi by Tripolitanian maritime merchants (King 1989; al-Idrisi).

Jadu-Libya.name: Jadu
Jadu-Libya.evidence_basis: Principal medieval Ibadi mountain town and fortified market of the western Jebel Nafusa documented through medieval Ibadi mosques, granaries, and Arabic geographical accounts (Prevost 2016; al-Idrisi).

Warrâq al-Hadar wa- Ambûba wa-Mît al-Nas.name: Warrâq al-Hadar wa- Ambûba wa-Mît al-Nasârâ

Tamdult-Morocco.name: Tamdult
Tamdult-Morocco.evidence_basis: Walled pre-Saharan silver-mining and caravan town surrounded by at least 5 km² of canal-irrigated gardens; thrived under the Almoravids and Almohads before abandonment in favour of Akka in the 15th century (González Villaescusa & Cressier 2011; Rosenberger 1970; Fenwick et al. 2022).

Massa-Morocco.name: Massa
Massa-Morocco.evidence_basis: Prominent Sous coastal ribat, pilgrimage shrine, and Atlantic/Saharan exchange settlement exporting ambergris, wax, and leather to Iberian traders (al-Bakri; al-Idrisi; Leo Africanus).

Awjila-Libya.name: Awjila
Awjila-Libya.evidence_basis: Ancient eastern Libyan Berber date-palm oasis anchoring the caravan route from Egypt and Siwa to Fezzan and Cyrenaica, featuring the medieval Atiq Mosque (al-Bakri; al-Idrisi; Leo Africanus).

Derna-Libya.name: Derna
Derna-Libya.evidence_basis: Modest spring-watered Cyrenaican coastal anchorage through most of the Middle Ages that experienced a sudden demographic surge after 1493 with the arrival of Andalusian refugees rebuilding its canal-irrigated gardens.

El Jadida-Morocco.name: El Jadida
El Jadida-Morocco.evidence_basis: Doukkala sheltered anchorage (Mazighan) serving regional wheat exports described by al-Idrisi and later fortified by the Portuguese in 1514 as the citadel of Mazagan.

El Oued-Algeria.name: El Oued
El Oued-Algeria.evidence_basis: Clustered sunken-palmery oasis settlement of the Grand Erg Oriental linking Biskra and Touggourt with the Tunisian Jarid and Ghadames caravan network.

Quseir al-Qadim-Egypt.name: Quseir al-Qadim
Quseir al-Qadim-Egypt.evidence_basis: Excavated Ayyubid and early Mamluk Red Sea trading port (coral-block and mudbrick settlement with Shaikh's House mercantile archive) serving Qus before silting caused relocation 8 km south to modern Quseir in the 15th century (Whitcomb & Johnson 1982; Peacock & Blue 2006).
